newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Tel Aviv Stock Exchange finishes stormy 1996.
newsitem.headline: Tel Aviv Stock Exchange finishes stormy 1996.

text.p: The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange experienced a stormy 1996, with falling share prices and trading volume and a dearth of new issues, but officials said on Wednesday they detected some silver linings.
"Its seems to me that anyone looking at the (exchange's annual statistical) brochure will see that it is too early to eulogise the bourse," managing director Saul Bronfeld said at a press conference.

Despite a rally in the final two months of the year, the market's broadest indicator, the general share index, fell 10.4 percent in 1996, marking the third year of the market's slump. Market capitalisation declined to 248.6 billion shekels at the end of the year from 255.3 billion shekels at the end of 1995.
The domestic new issues market raised just 1.278 billion shekels, compared with 2.167 billion shekels in 1995. Only seven new companies went public.

But Bronfeld noted some positive statistics, among them that average daily trading volume at 108 million shekels a day was still four times the 1988 level. At its peak in 1993, daily volume averaged 502 million shekels and in 1995 it was 130 million shekels.

The top six traded companies - Bank Hapoalim, Koor Industries, Bezeq Israel Telecom, Bank Leumi (BASLI.TA, Israel Chemicals CHIM.TA and IDB Holdings IDBH.TA - did not trade on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) eight years ago, he added.

Nevertheless, Bronfeld conceded that Israeli companies had been going public in large numbers overseas, particularly in the United States, rather than in Tel Aviv. He said that of some 80 Israeli companies floated in overseas in recent years, not one had sought a dual listing afterwards in Israel.
"The traffic between Tel Aviv and the United States is one way," he said.

Chairman Yair Orgler stressed the competitive threat to the exchange from the globalisation of capital markets. But he also cited domestic factors behind the TASE's woes, including a volatile economy and the run on provident funds in July and August.

Inflation rose to a 14.5 percent annual pace in the first half, then fell sharply, while the overall economy began slowing in the second half, he recalled. Short-term interest rates peaked at mid-year, although Orgler refused to comment on the impact rates were having on the market.

The run on the provident funds, which are long-term savings programmes, caused yields on inflation-indexed long bonds to rise as high as 5.3 percent in August, said Orgler. It also drew some 100 million shekels out of the securities market and into bank deposits.
"If part of this amount moves in the direction of the stock market, imagine what this will do," said Orgler. "This is one thing that holds a lot of potential for the bourse in the next year."
Orgler decried the lack of long-term institutional investors, particularly the absence of pension funds, which rely on non-tradable government bonds for the bulk of their portfolios.
"A stock market without institutional investors will have difficult fulfilling its role," he said.
